content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Signing Git Commits with GPG"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Signing your Git commits with GPG (GNU Privacy Guard) adds a layer of security and trust to your contributions. It allows others to verify that the commits were indeed made by you and haven't been tampered with. This tutorial will guide you through the process of generating a GPG key, configuring Git to use it, and signing your commits."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Prerequisites"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"GPG installed on your system. You can download it from 'https://www.gnupg.org/download/' or install it using your system's package manager (e.g., 'apt-get install gnupg2' on Debian/Ubuntu, 'brew install gnupg' on macOS)."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Git installed on your system."},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Generating a GPG Key"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"If you don't already have a GPG key, you'll need to generate one. Open your terminal and run the following command:"},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"gpg --gen-key"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Follow the prompts to select your desired key type, key size, and expiration date. It's recommended to use RSA and RSA (default) with a key size of 4096 bits. You'll also need to provide your name and email address. Finally, you'll be prompted to create a passphrase for your key. Choose a strong and memorable passphrase."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Listing Your GPG Keys"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"After generating your key, you need to find its key ID. Use the following command to list your GPG keys:"},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format long"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"The output will show your secret keys. Look for the line starting with 'sec' (secret key). The key ID is the 8-character string after the slash ('/'). For example, if the line is 'sec rsa4096/YOUR_KEY_ID', then 'YOUR_KEY_ID' is your key ID."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring Git to Use Your GPG Key"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Now, you need to tell Git to use your GPG key for signing commits. Use the following command, replacing 'YOUR_KEY_ID' with your actual key ID:"},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"git config --global user.signingkey YOUR_KEY_ID"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"You also need to tell Git which GPG program to use. This is usually 'gpg' or 'gpg2'. Use the following command:"},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"git config --global gpg.program gpg"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Signing Commits"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"To sign a single commit, use the '-S' flag when committing:"},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"git commit -S -m \"Your commit message\""},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"You'll be prompted to enter your GPG key passphrase. After entering it, your commit will be signed."},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"To automatically sign all commits, you can configure Git to do so. Use the following command:"},{"order":24,"type":"code","text":"git config --global commit.gpgsign true"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"With this setting enabled, all commits will be signed automatically. You'll still be prompted for your GPG key passphrase for each commit."},{"order":26,"type":"subheading","text":"Verifying Signed Commits"},{"order":27,"type":"paragraph","text":"To verify a signed commit, use the following command:"},{"order":28,"type":"code","text":"git log --show-signature"},{"order":29,"type":"paragraph","text":"This will display the commit history, including the GPG signature status. A 'Good signature' message indicates that the commit was signed with a valid GPG key. If you see 'BAD signature', it means the signature is invalid or the key is not trusted."},{"order":30,"type":"subheading","text":"Trusting GPG Keys"},{"order":31,"type":"paragraph","text":"If you see a 'BAD signature' message because the key is not trusted, you need to import and trust the key. First, get the key from a keyserver:"},{"order":32,"type":"code","text":"gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys YOUR_KEY_ID"},{"order":33,"type":"paragraph","text":"Then, trust the key:"},{"order":34,"type":"code","text":"gpg --edit-key YOUR_KEY_ID"},{"order":35,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the GPG command prompt, type 'trust' and follow the prompts to set the trust level. Choose a level that reflects your confidence in the key's owner. Finally, type 'quit' to exit the GPG command prompt."},{"order":36,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":37,"type":"paragraph","text":"Signing your Git commits with GPG is a valuable practice for ensuring the integrity and authenticity of your contributions. By following these steps, you can enhance the security of your Git workflow and build trust with your collaborators."}]
